title: Stratified Sampling and Allocation
breadcrumb: Sampling theory → Stratified sampling → Estimation and allocation
engineName: Stratification divides the population into non-overlapping groups and samples each group separately.
objectives: Construct stratified estimators of a population mean and total.
Calculate variance under independent SRSWOR within strata.
Distinguish proportional, equal and Neyman allocation.
Allocate a fixed sample under unequal stratum sizes and variability.
Explain how finite-population corrections and costs affect allocation.

prereq.name: Finite population
prereq.why: The target is a fixed population partitioned into strata.

prereq.name: Sample mean and variance
prereq.why: Each stratum has its own sample mean and variance.

prereq.name: Expectation and variance
prereq.why: The combined design variance adds independent stratum contributions.

traps: Use population shares W_h, not sample shares, in the combined mean.
Neyman allocation uses N_hS_h when unit costs are equal.
A stratum census has zero sampling variance.
Stratification does not guarantee a variance reduction for every partition.
howto: List strata and their population sizes. Compute W_h=N_h/N. Estimate the mean with population-weighted stratum means. For variance, retain each stratum's own sampling fraction and variance. Choose allocation only after stating whether the objective is equal, proportional or variance-oriented and whether unit costs differ.

scenes.title: Partition the population
body: A stratified design divides the target population into non-overlapping groups before sampling.
Every eligible unit belongs to exactly one stratum. The strata together cover the target population.
A sample is selected separately within each stratum. This guarantees representation of each group and allows allocation to reflect population size or variability.

refresh: Define the group before selecting the sample.
A region, age band or institution type can define a stratum.
A stratum is a population subgroup, not a selected cluster.
No unit should belong to two strata.
Overlapping groups do not form a partition.
Check the frame for duplicate membership.

items.ask: Must all target units be covered?
refresh: Every eligible unit must be covered.
An omitted unit has zero chance of selection.
Check the frame for omissions and duplicates.

ask.q: What two properties define a valid partition?

scenes.title: Why stratify?
scenes.body: A population may contain distinct groups with different average values. A simple random sample can, by chance, include too few units from a small but important group. Stratification ensures each group is represented. Precision can improve when units within each stratum are relatively similar, while stratum means differ. This is a potential gain, not a guarantee: the result depends on the variable, the partition and the allocation.

scenario.title: Representation before estimation
scenario.body: A survey covers two districts. District A has 100 households and District B has 200. Water use varies substantially between districts, but households within each district have similar use. A stratified sample selects households separately in both districts. The final population mean must weight each district's sample mean by its share of the 300 households. Equal sample sizes would not make the districts equally important in the population estimate. This example separates the estimator weights from the sample allocation.
scenario.answer: It can reduce within-stratum variation while ensuring that each group is represented.

ask.nudge: The population sizes of the strata.

scenes.title: Population weights

viz.caption: N₁=100 and N₂=200: population shares are 1/3 and 2/3.

scenes.body: Let N be the total population size and N_h the size of stratum h. The population share is W_h=N_h/N. These weights sum to one. They remain the correct weights for the overall mean even when the sample allocation is disproportionate.

ask.q: If stratum means are 10 and 20, what is the combined mean for these shares?

scenes.title: Estimator and variance
scenes.objective: Derive the mean, total and variance estimators.

blocks.body: There are L strata. N_h and n_h are the population and sample sizes. W_h=N_h/N, f_h=n_h/N_h, and ȳ_h and S_h² are the sample mean and finite-population variance in stratum h.
ȳ_st=Σ_h W_hȳ_h. The total estimator is Ŷ_st=Σ_h N_hȳ_h=Nȳ_st.
Under independent SRSWOR within strata, V(ȳ_st)=Σ_h W_h²(1−f_h)S_h²/n_h. Therefore V(Ŷ_st)=N²V(ȳ_st).
Replace S_h² by the within-stratum sample variance s_h²: v(ȳ_st)=Σ_h W_h²(1−f_h)s_h²/n_h.

scenes.flow: Partition population → sample independently within strata → calculate each ȳ_h → weight by W_h → add variance contributions.

ask.q: Why are the weights W_h and not n_h/n?
ask.nudge: The target is the population mean, so weights represent population shares.

scenes.title: Worked example: proportional allocation
scenes.problem: N₁=100, N₂=200, S₁=4, S₂=6 and total sample n=30. Use proportional allocation and calculate V(ȳ_st).

steps.say: The total population is 300, so the population shares are one-third and two-thirds.
The sampling fractions are both one-tenth.
Substitute the values into the stratified variance formula.
The standard error is the square root.

scenes.after: The population weights determine the combined mean; allocation determines the precision.

scenes.intro: Try each prompt before revealing its answer.

scenes.title: Complete Neyman allocation
scenes.objective: Allocate a sample using stratum sizes and standard deviations.
scenes.problem: N₁=100, S₁=4; N₂=200, S₂=6; n=30; equal unit costs. Complete the Neyman allocation.

steps.hint: Multiply population size by standard deviation.

scenes.after: Check that rounded allocations sum to n and do not exceed stratum sizes.

ask.q: Why does stratum 2 receive three times the continuous allocation?
ask.nudge: Its N_hS_h weight is three times as large.

scenes.title: Compare allocation rules
scenes.objective: Distinguish equal, proportional and Neyman allocation.

blocks.body: n_h≈n/L. Each stratum receives approximately the same sample size.
n_h=nN_h/N=nW_h. Every stratum has the same sampling fraction.
For equal unit costs, n_h=nN_hS_h/(Σ_g N_gS_g). It accounts for both population size and variability.
With per-unit cost c_h and a fixed variable-cost budget, the continuous variance-oriented allocation is proportional to N_hS_h/√c_h, subject to feasibility and minimum-sample constraints.

ask.q: Which allocation uses within-stratum standard deviations?

scenes.title: Guided comparison
scenes.problem: For N₁=100, N₂=200, S₁=4, S₂=6 and n=30, find both allocations.
hints: Round only after finding the continuous allocation.
scenes.answer: Proportional: (10,20). Neyman: (7.5,22.5), with feasible rounding such as (8,22).
scenes.check: Both allocations sum to 30; the Neyman weights are 400 and 1200.

scenario.title: Two districts, one field team
scenario.body: A team can complete 30 interviews. District A contains 100 households and has a target-variable standard deviation of 4. District B contains 200 households and standard deviation 6. Interview costs are equal. The manager asks for a population-proportional allocation and a variance-oriented allocation. The first uses population sizes only; the second uses both population size and variability. The final integer allocation must preserve the total workload and respect each district's available population.
scenario.q: Which rule uses the standard deviations?

solution.say: Proportional shares are one-third and two-thirds, giving 10 and 20.
The continuous Neyman allocation is 7.5 and 22.5.
A feasible rounded allocation is 8 and 22.

ask.q: What assumption supports ordinary Neyman allocation?
ask.nudge: Equal per-unit costs and a fixed total sample size.

scenes.title: Check common traps
scenes.objective: Identify incorrect weighting and allocation claims.

items.claim: The stratified mean uses sample shares n_h/n.

items.why: The sampling fraction is calculated within stratum h.

items.claim: Proportional allocation gives equal sampling fractions.
Neyman allocation is proportional to N_hS_h for equal costs.
items.why: It accounts for population size and standard deviation.

items.claim: A stratum sampled by census contributes zero sampling variance.
items.why: Its sampling fraction is one, so the FPC is zero.
The gain depends on the strata, variable and allocation.

scenes.title: Transfer: unequal costs
scenes.problem: Two strata have N₁S₁=600 and N₂S₂=1200. Costs are c₁=1 and c₂=4. Find n₁:n₂ under a fixed variable-cost budget.

solution.say: Divide each N_hS_h by the square root of its cost.

ask.q: Why does the more expensive stratum not receive more sample?
ask.nudge: Its higher cost offsets its larger size-variability weight.

scenes.title: Final checklist
scenes.body: A valid stratification partitions the population into non-overlapping groups. Under independent SRSWOR within strata, estimate the mean by Σ_hW_hȳ_h and the total by Σ_hN_hȳ_h. The variance of the mean is Σ_hW_h²(1−f_h)S_h²/n_h. Proportional allocation follows N_h. Neyman allocation follows N_hS_h when costs are equal. With unequal costs, use N_hS_h/√c_h. Check the population weights, FPCs, sample-size total and feasibility.

scenes.title: Mastery check
scenes.objective: Demonstrate independent command of stratified sampling.

tricks: Write population weights before combining means.
Round only after the continuous allocation.
shortcuts: Proportional allocation gives equal sampling fractions.
Check that population weights sum to one.
remember: Ordinary Neyman allocation assumes equal costs.
